title: Shabbat with children
hookLine: games, stories and a special dessert make the day a delight
tomorrow: a Muslim friend asks if Shabbat is like Friday prayers. is it?

cards: Friday, half past five. Dinner is late, one kid is upside down on the couch, the other is crying about the wrong color cup, and the candles still have to be lit.

Ask a kid what's special about a Tuesday and you get a shrug. Ask about the night with the dessert that only comes on Friday, and you get a list. So what does the tradition hand a tired grown-up at half past five?
A job for every child, and a blessing with hands on their heads.

teach.b: In homes that keep the custom, parents or grandparents put their hands on each child's head on Friday night and bless them.
For boys, the words come from Genesis, where Jacob blesses his two grandsons: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." For girls: may God make you like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah.
Then the priestly blessing: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." Why Ephraim and Manasseh, not the well-known patriarchs? Some readers say because they're brothers in Genesis who don't fight.
Others say because they grew up far from home, in Egypt, and stayed who they were. Either way, here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the weekly blessing names two grandsons.
And the rest of the evening can be built around the children too. They can set out the candlesticks, pour the grape juice, lift the cloth off the challah, choose the song.
Some families save one dessert, one story or one board game for Shabbat only, so the day has a taste and a shape a child can wait for.
None of that is a bribe, and none of it needs to be fancy: a bowl of grapes that only appears on Friday works.
The Shabbat table was always meant to be a delight, and children, it turns out, already know how to do that.

how: On Friday night, in homes that keep the custom, parents bless each child with hands on the head, using Jacob's blessing or the matriarchs' names and the priestly blessing; children often help light, pour and uncover the challah, and families keep special foods or games for Shabbat.

at home, at the table, by parents or grandparents.

games.q: your sister's kids, six and nine, groan when Friday dinner runs long. she asks how to make them want it. what fits the tradition?
o: give them jobs, a blessing with hands on their heads, and a treat only Shabbat brings.
shorten everything and skip the blessings so they can leave the table sooner.
explain every rule of Shabbat clearly, so they understand why it matters.
games.why: the tradition builds the evening around children: their own blessing, their own jobs, a taste they wait for. understanding can grow later; delight comes first.

practice: Bring to mind one child in your life, or the child you once were. Plan one Shabbat treat for them: a dessert, a story, a game, saved only for that night. Say the plan out loud once, quietly, the way you'd make a promise.

wordCard.voice: Shabbat with children: jobs for small hands, a blessing with hands on their heads, and a treat only this night brings.

orig.note: Hebrew: the blessing of the children, given at home on Friday night.

carryVoice: Your line: children love this day. With a job in it, they'll wait for it all week. See you tomorrow.
